## Serum GGT as a biomarker of metabolic stress: current evidence

**Biological basis.** GGT is a cell-membrane enzyme central to glutathione (GSH) metabolism ?€? it hydrolyzes extracellular GSH to supply cysteine for intracellular GSH resynthesis, making it a first-line defense against oxidative stress. The relationship is paradoxical, though: while GGT supports antioxidant capacity, experimental work shows that GGT activity can also catalyze reactive oxygen species generation in the presence of iron or other transition metals, meaning elevated GGT can reflect ongoing oxidative burden rather than just protective capacity (ScienceDirect, "The dark side of gamma-glutamyltransferase"; Free Radical Research review). Within its normal range, serum GGT positively predicts F2-isoprostanes (a marker of lipid oxidative damage) and inflammatory markers, supporting GGT as a proxy for systemic oxidative stress rather than a purely hepatobiliary marker.

**Association with metabolic syndrome.** A systematic review and dose-response meta-analysis (Pubmed, 2015) established that GGT is positively associated with metabolic syndrome risk across populations, and this has been reaffirmed repeatedly since ?€? most recently a 2025 study in adolescents (Esmaeili et al., *Endocrinology, Diabetes & Metabolism*) found elevated GGT significantly associated with higher odds of metabolic syndrome and central obesity, reinforcing GGT as useful for early detection even before adulthood. A 2024 paper proposed GGT as a biomarker specifically for pancreatic steatosis in patients with concurrent obesity, insulin resistance, and MASLD ?€? extending its role beyond the liver to broader ectopic fat deposition.
